sim:valley-stability:
Simulator Valley of stability: beta-stability curve vs integer lattice. This visualization frames the valley of stability as a Diophantine approximation problem.

Controls:

  • q slider: Varies the substrate parameter from 1.0 (classical, no Coulomb) to 2.0 (deep quantum). Default: the substrate q.
  • View: Toggles between the (p, n)-plane and the (A, n/p)-plane.

Display:

  • Blue curve: Continuous beta-stability line p^*(A) = A/(2 + cA^{2/3}) from the Skein binding Lagrangian.
  • Green dots: Integer lattice points (p_{\mathrm{stab}}, n_{\mathrm{stab}}) for observed stable isotopes.
  • Red segments: Diophantine error \varepsilon(A) (vertical distance from each lattice point to the curve).
  • Gold diamonds: Stability pairs (shell closures).
  • Shaded band: Valley width (range of p values within one beta-decay half-life of the stable isotope).

As q \to 1, the curve straightens to p = A/2. All lattice points fall on this diagonal. The Diophantine problem becomes trivial. As q increases, the curve bends, lattice points scatter, and the stability-pair structure emerges.
sec:nuclear-stability-decay-intro:
Isotopes displaced from the Diophantine valley of stability relax toward the valley floor through weak transitions. In the skein calculus on H_A(q), a \beta-decay transition is a single crossing-change surgery on the Gröbner–Shirshov normal form of the nuclear braid, subject to conservation of the categorical lepton number.

This section defines the \beta-decay skein transition and categorical lepton number, proves the continuant recurrence governing the charged-lepton mass tower and \tau-leptonic universality, and derives parity violation (\mathrm{V}-\mathrm{A} chirality selection), proposed by Lee and Yang [lee-yang-1956] and observed in nuclear \beta-decay by Wu, Ambler, Hayward, Hoppes and Hudson [wu1957parity], directly from the q \neq 1 asymmetry of the Hecke quadratic relation (\sigma_i - q)(\sigma_i + q^{-1}) = 0, concluding with nuclear spin–parity J^\pi selection rules.
def:beta-decay-skein:
Definition Beta decay as a Skein crossing change on the Gröbner normal form. Beta decay inserts the weak-force torus knot T_{3,5} at the converting quark of a nuclear Gröbner–Shirshov normal form \mathcal{N}(Z, N). The braid word is \beta_{T_{3,5}} = (\sigma_1\sigma_2)^5. It has 10 crossings. The operation concludes with re-reduction. The emitted electron is the word e^- = \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 (electron), whose closure is the Hopf link; the positron is e^+ = \sigma_0^{-1}\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma_0^{-1} (positron). Written in the generators \sigma_0, \sigma_1 of the electron word, the vertex is (\sigma_0\sigma_1)^5, and it carries the electron word as a braid factor:

  (\sigma_0\sigma_1)^5 = e^- \cdot \bigl(e^- \cdot (\sigma_0\sigma_1)^2\bigr) \quad\text{in } B_3 ,

so the 10 letters split into the 3 of e^- and a positive residue of 7.

A \beta^- transition inserts the T_{3,5} braid at the converting \mathfrak{d}-quark crossing of \mathcal{N}(Z, N), followed by re-reduction:

  \mathcal{N}(Z, N) \cdot \beta_{T_{3,5}}
  \xrightarrow{ \text{reduce}}
  \mathcal{N}(Z + 1,  N - 1)
  \sqcup
  e^-
  \sqcup
  K_{0_1}^{\sigma}.

A \beta^+ transition is the mirror operation. It inserts the conjugate T_{3,5}^{\sigma} braid with q \leftrightarrow q^{-1}:

  \mathcal{N}(Z, N) \cdot \beta_{T_{3,5}}^{\sigma}
  \xrightarrow{ \text{reduce}}
  \mathcal{N}(Z - 1,  N + 1)
  \sqcup
  e^+
  \sqcup
  K_{0_1}.
rem:beta-decay-skein-properties:
Remark Weak vertex, 10-crossing budget, and Q-value of the \beta-decay Skein operation. The \beta-decay Skein operation requires the T_{3,5} weak vertex, the 10-crossing budget, the \mathbb{Z}/2 involution relating \beta^\pm, the lepton-pair decomposition, and the 10-crossing Q-value.

Setup. A nucleus \mathcal{N}(Z, N) is a satellite link of A = Z + N Borromean components. Its braid word in B_{3A} reduces to a unique Gröbner–Shirshov normal form \mathcal{N}(Z, N) in the Iwahori–Hecke algebra H_{3A}(q).

Each nucleon is a Borromean link \mathcal{B}_3(q_1, q_2, q_3) with quark strands:

  • Proton: \mathfrak{p} = \mathcal{B}_3(\mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{d})
  • Neutron: \mathfrak{n} = \mathcal{B}_3(\mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{d}, \mathfrak{d})

The crossing type at each generator \sigma_i depends on the quark flavours of the two strands. The \mathfrak{u}\text{-}\mathfrak{u} crossing is positive. The \mathfrak{d}\text{-}\mathfrak{d} crossing is negative. The \mathfrak{u}\text{-}\mathfrak{d} crossing is mixed.
def:lepton-number-categorical:
Definition Categorical Lepton Number. Lepton number is the count of Skein smoothings applied to the nuclear normal form.

Let \mathcal{N} be a nuclear link in Gröbner–Shirshov normal form. Let \mathcal{N}' be obtained from \mathcal{N} by a sequence of k Skein crossing changes. The lepton number of this transition is L = k.
rem:lepton-number-categorical-properties:
Remark Conservation, \mathbb{Z}-grading, and the \chi = -6 constraint on lepton number. The categorical lepton number possesses several structural properties.

Each beta decay applies the Skein relation at one crossing. This produces a smoothing L_0^{\pm}. It contains exactly one lepton–antilepton pair. Lepton number counts these smoothings.

Each smoothing L_0^{\pm} contributes:

  • One charged lepton (e^- = \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 or e^+ = \sigma_0^{-1}\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma_0^{-1}) with lepton number \pm 1.
  • One neutrino or antineutrino (K_{0_1} or K_{0_1}^{\sigma}) with lepton number -1.

The net lepton number of each L_0^{\pm} pair is zero.

Conservation. Lepton number is conserved by construction:

  1. Skein smoothings produce lepton pairs with net lepton number 0. The nuclear sector loses one crossing. Hadrons carry lepton number 0. The total is \Delta L = 0.
  2. Gröbner–Shirshov re-reduction acts within the Iwahori–Hecke algebra. It produces no smoothings. The total is \Delta L = 0.
  3. Markov moves change the braid representative but not the link type. The total is \Delta L = 0.

Every process expressed as a sequence of Skein relations and Hecke reductions conserves lepton number.

Lepton number is not a \mathbb{Z}-grading (proved). The Skein module \mathcal{K}(S^3; q) admits no \mathbb{Z}-grading by the smoothing count with the nuclear sector in grade 0 and each smoothing shifting the grade by +1.

The skein relation is inhomogeneous for such a grading. Writing it as

  L_+ - L_- = (q - q^{-1})\,L_0 ,

the left-hand side is a difference of grade-g classes, hence grade g, while the right-hand side carries one further smoothing, hence grade g+1 (scalars are grade-preserving). An element lying in two distinct homogeneous components is 0, so the relation forces (q - q^{-1})L_0 = 0 and L_+ = L_-. Imposing the grading therefore annihilates every smoothing: it would make lepton number identically 0, which is the one value it cannot take.

This is a scope-(b) exclusion of one construction, with its invariant cited (the defining disjointness of homogeneous components); it does not touch lepton number itself, the Skein module, or the Y = B - L route.

What this leaves, and where L does live. An inhomogeneous relation is what a filtration tolerates rather than a grading, but the Vassiliev filtration grades invariants v : K \to R, not states, so it does not by itself supply a state-valued L.

The carrier is the braid word, not the knot type. This is forced: L cannot factor through the unframed knot type, since the mirror must move the carrier and the unknot is amphichiral. It is also the convention of Antiparticles from crossing reversal, which takes the mirror to be \sigma_i \mapsto \sigma_i^{-1} on braid words and records that it preserves the knot type.

The braid words are \nu_e = \sigma_1 and, by the electron ruling (electron), e^- = \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0, with antiparticles \sigma_1^{-1} and \sigma_0^{-1}\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma_0^{-1} --- distinct braid words (the neutrino words close to the unknot, the electron words to the positive and negative Hopf links), which is exactly how the mirror acts freely. Both electron words have writhe \pm 3, as \sigma_1^{\pm 3} did, so the signs below are unchanged. The writhes follow from the words, and the candidate

  L(\beta) = \mathrm{sign}\bigl(\mathrm{writhe}(\beta)\bigr)

reproduces every row of the table below, hadrons included. It is a candidate, not a derivation: \mathrm{sign} is a choice of function, the quark braid word is still absent from the corpus, and chirality (u_L vs u_R) is not yet represented.

And it is refuted, under both readings of the gauge freedom.

Markov II. Stabilisation raises the writhe by 1 without changing the link, so L jumps from 0 to 1 on the baryon --- violating conservation clause 3 above, which requires \Delta L = 0 under Markov moves .

The minimal-level ruling. The escape from the first refutation was that states are Gröbner--Shirshov normal forms, with the observable evaluated at the lowest level of the substrate tower. That closes the escape rather than opening it. The table above assigns \nu_e = K_{0_1} = T_{2,1}, the unknot, whose braid index is 1: its minimal-level normal form is the empty word, and so is its mirror's. At the level where the framework says observables live, \nu_e and \nu_e^{\sigma} are the same state, and no function of the state can give them +1 and -1 --- quite apart from \mathrm{sign}(0) = 0 \neq +1. This is proved, and it is the same obstruction established above for the unframed knot type, reappearing once the canonical representative is pinned.

So the "carrier is the braid word, not the knot type" escape is unavailable at minimal level, where the braid word is determined by the knot type. Scope-(a): L = \mathrm{sign}(w) is refuted; lepton number itself and the Y = B - L route are untouched, and what the refutation locates is that L must come from data the writhe does not carry --- the framing or the smoothing history, not the crossing sum.

The \chi = -6 constraint. In the Descartes universe, the Euler characteristic \chi_{\mathrm{eu}}(M_0) = -6 constrains Bring's surface. The torus knot generators T(2, n) with odd n \leq 7 exhaust the fermion spectrum. In the backup model the electron (T_{2,3}) and neutrino (K_{0_1} = T_{2,1}) are the lowest torus knots in this sequence, and the argument read the smoothing L_0^{-} as decomposing into exactly these single-component closures. This selection does not hold for the ruled electron. The closure of \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 is the Hopf link, which has two components and is not a T(2,n) with odd n. So the \chi = -6 constraint, as stated, does not select the electron. Scope-(a): this is a statement about this argument, not about lepton number, whose conservation clauses above do not use it.

Structural origin of lepton-number conservation. In the Standard Model, lepton number conservation is an accidental symmetry. Here, it is a structural invariant. The Skein relation is the unique operation that changes crossing type. It always produces exactly one lepton pair. The Iwahori–Hecke algebra contains no mechanism to produce an odd number of leptons. The smoothing is a topological operation on a single crossing. Each smoothing is binary.

Lepton number violation requires a process that changes crossing type without passing through the Skein relation. Such a process must exist outside the Iwahori–Hecke algebra. In the \chi = -6 universe, no such process exists.
prop:lepton-continuant-recurrence: Proposition Continuant recurrence for the lepton tower T_{2,n}. The charged lepton tower T_{2,n} for n = 3, 5, 7 describes the e^-, \mu^-, \tau^- generations. It possesses a closed-form normal form in H_2(q) \subset H_3(q). A Morgan–Voyce continuant recurrence defines this form.
prf:lepton-continuant-recurrence:
Proof Proof of lepton continuant recurrence. The Hecke relation \sigma_0^2 = (q - q^{-1}) \sigma_0 + \mathbf{1} yields:

  \sigma_0^{n+1}
  = \sigma_0 \cdot \sigma_0^n
  = \sigma_0 (a_n \cdot \mathbf{1} + b_n \cdot \sigma_0)
  = a_n  \sigma_0 + b_n  \sigma_0^2
  = a_n  \sigma_0 + b_n ((q - q^{-1}) \sigma_0 + \mathbf{1})
  = b_n \cdot \mathbf{1} + (a_n + h  b_n) \cdot \sigma_0.

Extracting the coefficients gives a_{n+1} = b_n and b_{n+1} = a_n + h b_n = b_{n-1} + h b_n. The initial conditions a_0 = 1, b_0 = 0 represent the identity. The initial conditions a_1 = 0, b_1 = 1 represent the single generator. This completes the induction.
rem:lepton-continuant-recurrence-novelty: Remark Mathematical novelty of the Morgan-Voyce lepton-tower continuant. The structural identification of the lepton-tower sequence as a positive-sign Morgan–Voyce continuant distinguishes it from standard Chebyshev U_n recurrences. This provides an algebraic framework that captures the combinatorial constraints of the lepton sector.

prop:tau-leptonic-universality: Proposition Lepton universality from the T_{3,5} weak vertex. The tau lepton decays leptonically via the T_{3,5} weak vertex. The factorized model sets the squared matrix element to |\mathcal{M}|^2 = |\mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Markov}}(T_{3,5})|^2. This amplitude is independent of the daughter lepton. It predicts lepton universality directly from the underlying Iwahori–Hecke algebra structure.
prf:tau-leptonic-universality:
Proof Proof of tau leptonic universality. Sketch.

The T_{3,5} weak vertex acts as a mediator between the parent tau T_{2,7} and the daughter lepton T_{2,n_\ell}. In the Iwahori--Hecke algebra H_3(q), one may form the product T_{2,n_\ell} \cdot T_{3,5} \cdot T_{2,7} and reduce to normal form. However, the correct physical amplitude is not this product trace.

The key observation is that the weak vertex creates the daughter lepton (preserving the topological quantum number), rather than composing with it. The T_{3,5} braid mediates the crossing change. The daughter lepton T_{2,n_\ell} and the two neutrinos (\nu = \mathbf{1}) are produced as separate link components. The transition amplitude therefore factorises:

  \mathcal{M}(\tau \to \ell\bar\nu\nu_\tau)
  = 
  \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Markov}}(T_{3,5})
   \times 
  (\text{kinematic factors depending on } m_\ell).

Because \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Markov}}(T_{3,5}) is independent of which daughter lepton is created, the matrix element |\mathcal{M}|^2 cancels in the ratio. This leaves only the phase-space factor f(m_\ell^2 / m_\tau^2).

Contrast with the product model. If one instead defines the amplitude as \mathrm{tr}_3(T_{2,n_\ell} \cdot T_{3,5} \cdot T_{2,7}), the non-commutativity of H_3(q) introduces a daughter-dependent correction that breaks universality: |\mathcal{M}_e|^2 / |\mathcal{M}_\mu|^2 \approx 0.69 \neq 1. The product model treats the daughter as composed with the vertex rather than created by it. This violates the topological separation of link components demanded by the Skein decomposition (lepton number). \square

prop:parity-violation-skein:
Proposition Parity non-conservation from the Skein relation at q \neq 1. Parity is violated by the weak interaction if and only if q \neq 1.

The Skein relation is invariant under parity \mathcal{P}: L_+ \leftrightarrow L_- if and only if q = 1. For any q \neq 1, the weak interaction violates parity.
prf:parity-violation-skein: Proof Proof of parity violation skein. The Skein relation assigns coefficient q to [L_+] and q^{-1} to [L_-]. Parity exchanges L_+ \leftrightarrow L_- but preserves q. The relation is \mathcal{P}-invariant if and only if q = q^{-1}. Since q > 0, this requires q = 1. \square
rem:parity-violation-skein-interpretatio:
Remark Physical interpretation: maximal parity violation and CP. The Hecke relation \sigma^2 = (q - q^{-1})\sigma + 1 breaks the symmetry between positive and negative crossings. At q = 1, \sigma^2 = 1. Parity is conserved. At the substrate parameter q_0, the relation becomes \sigma^2 = 0.209\,\sigma + 1. The 0.209\,\sigma term distinguishes positive from negative crossings. This violates parity.

The Hecke deformation parameter controls the degree of parity violation:

  q - q^{-1} = 0.209 \quad (\text{at } q = q_0).

All parity violation traces back to q \neq 1.

Maximal parity violation.

The Standard Model weak force violates parity maximally. It couples only to left-handed particles. This maps to crossing chirality. A positive crossing \sigma_i contributes weight q to the categorical action. A negative crossing \sigma_i^{-1} contributes q^{-1}. The ratio q^2 = 1.232 measures the left-right asymmetry.

The Wu experiment found a strong forward-backward asymmetry in {}^{60}\mathrm{Co} beta decay. This asymmetry represents the crossing chirality of the nuclear link. The {}^{60}\mathrm{Co} braid word carries a specific writhe w \neq 0. The Skein crossing change at q_0 produces an emission pattern determined by q^w.

Connection to the \mathbb{Z}/2 of beta decay.

The involution q \leftrightarrow q^{-1} exchanges \beta^- \leftrightarrow \beta^+. It acts as the combined \widehat{CP} operation. It applies parity \mathcal{P} by mirroring all crossings. It applies charge conjugation \hat{C} by exchanging the electron e^- = \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 with the positron e^+ = \sigma_0^{-1}\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma_0^{-1}.

  • \mathcal{P} alone is violated because q \neq q^{-1}.
  • \hat{C} alone is violated because the electron and positron differ in mass ordering.
  • \widehat{CP} is conserved to leading order because q \leftrightarrow q^{-1} is a symmetry of the Iwahori–Hecke algebra.
prop:nuclear-spin-parity:
Proposition Nuclear spin is integral for even A and half-integral for odd A. The nuclear spin quantum number J is integral when A is even and half-integral when A is odd.

This follows topologically from the braid representation. Each nucleon is a spin-\tfrac{1}{2} fermion. It is a single-component knot. The tensor product of A such representations dictates a spin parity determined by A \bmod 2.

Let \mathcal{N}(Z, N) be a nucleus with mass number A = Z + N. The total angular momentum J satisfies:

  J \in \mathbb{Z} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad A \in 2\mathbb{Z}
  J \in \mathbb{Z} + \tfrac{1}{2} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad A \in 2\mathbb{Z} + 1

prf:nuclear-spin-parity:
Proof Proof of nuclear spin parity. Each nucleon—proton \mathfrak{p} = \mathcal{B}_3(\mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{d}) or neutron \mathfrak{n} = \mathcal{B}_3(\mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{d}, \mathfrak{d})—is a knot (a single-component link closure of the Borromean braid). Knots carry half-integral spin; links carry integral spin.

The nuclear link \mathcal{N}(Z, N) is a satellite of A Borromean knots joined by Hopf links. In \mathrm{SU}_q(2) representation theory, the tensor product of A spin-\tfrac{1}{2} representations decomposes as:

  \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\otimes A}
  = 
  \bigoplus_{J = J_{\min}}^{A/2} V_J^{\oplus m_J}

Here, J_{\min} = 0 for even A and J_{\min} = \tfrac{1}{2} for odd A. Every summand V_J shares the parity (J \bmod 1) of A/2 \bmod 1. This standard result holds for all q > 0. The q-deformation preserves the spin parity of tensor products.

Explicitly, the q-Clebsch--Gordan decomposition V_{1/2} \otimes V_J = V_{J+1/2} \oplus V_{J-1/2} (for J \geq 1/2) adds \tfrac{1}{2} at each step. After A tensor factors, the spin parity equals A/2 \bmod 1. \square

The braid group perspective. In the braid group B_A, the writhe w(\beta) of the standard nuclear braid representative has parity:

  w(\beta) \equiv \binom{A}{2} \pmod{2}.

Writhe parity determines statistics:

  • w even \Leftrightarrow bosonic statistics \Leftrightarrow J \in \mathbb{Z}.
  • w odd \Leftrightarrow fermionic statistics \Leftrightarrow J \in \mathbb{Z} + \tfrac{1}{2}.

Since \binom{A}{2} = A(A-1)/2, the writhe is even if and only if A \equiv 0 or 1 \pmod{4}. However, the q-deformed spin-statistics theorem follows directly from representation theory, independent of writhe.

The Jones--Wenzl projector. In the Temperley--Lieb algebra TL_A(\delta) with \delta = -(q^{1/2} + q^{-1/2}), the Jones--Wenzl projector p_A projects onto the highest-weight irreducible representation V_{A/2}. The embedding of the nuclear link in the TL algebra and the action of p_A determine the ground state spin.

For {}^{14}\mathrm{N} (A = 14, even), the ground state has J = 1. The projector p_{14} projects onto V_7, but the nuclear link's embedding selects the J = 1 subrepresentation via the coupling pattern of 7 protons and 7 neutrons.

Key examples. See Table.

The integer spin (J = 1) of {}^{14}\mathrm{N} ruled out the pre-1932 proton-electron nuclear model, which predicted 21 fermions (14 protons, 7 electrons) and half-integer spin. Neutrons as spin-\tfrac{1}{2} particles resolved this, giving 14 nucleons and integer spin.

In this framework, this is automatic. Both the proton and neutron are spin-\tfrac{1}{2} knots. They share the Borromean topology but differ in quark colouring. Thus, 14 half-integer spins couple to an integer total spin.
rem:nuclear-spin-parity-novelty: Remark Mathematical novelty of the \mathrm{SU}_q(2) spin-parity synthesis. Formulating parity strictly via \mathrm{SU}_q(2) tensor-product rules algebraically embeds empirical parity constraints within the theory. This reproduces standard spin-statistics without external postulates.
sec:nuclear-stability-decay-hadron-half-:
Whereas the imaginary part of the complex volume \mathfrak{Q}_\beta = \operatorname{Im}\mathfrak{V} determines the reaction endpoint energy of a \beta-decay transition, the decay rate \Gamma = \ln 2 / t_{1/2} is governed by the squared matrix element of the skein transition operator combined with the phase-space integral.

This section identifies the squared \beta-decay matrix element with a ratio of parent and daughter Markov traces, in which the exponential growth of each trace cancels, derives the categorical hadron half-life formula, proves the q-self-correction theorem accounting for the leading deviation from the classical Fermi fifth-power law, and incorporates the skein–Coulomb enhancement factor for charged final states. Combining Gröbner–Shirshov normal-form reduction with Kummer \mu_n-torsion shell closure yields the skein shell-correction tables across the light and intermediate \beta-emitters.
prop:trace-ratio-observable:
Proposition The physical observable: ratio of Markov-traced generator volumes. The Markov trace of the nuclear braid is a link invariant that grows exponentially with A (Markov trace factorization). The physical observable — the transition matrix element |\mathcal{M}_q|^2 — is the ratio of parent and daughter traces, where the exponential growth cancels.

The beta-decay matrix element squared is proportional to the ratio of Markov-traced generator volumes at the affected generators:

  |\mathcal{M}_q|^2
   \propto 
  \prod_{i=0}^{p}
  \left|
    \frac{\hat{V}_i^{\mathrm{par}}}{\hat{V}_i^{\mathrm{dau}}}
  \right|^2

where \hat{V}_i = z \cdot a_i + b_i is the Markov-traced generator volume at \sigma_i. The product runs only over generators i \leq p (those affected by the conversion of nucleon p from neutron to proton). Generators i > p cancel exactly between parent and daughter.

Archimedean specialisation. What follows sits on the archimedean side of the substrate wall. It invokes real- or complex-analytic constructs — real-valued physical observables, real-analytic bounds, transcendental constants, or numerical evaluation at the substrate parameter q_0. Any generic categorical / q-deformation identities it draws on remain valid over an abstract coefficient ring; only their archimedean realization is specialized here.
prf:trace-ratio-observable:
Proof Proof of trace ratio observable. From the factorization theorem:

  \frac{\mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{N}(Z, N))}
       {\mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{N}(p+1, n-1))}
  = 
  \frac{\prod_{i=0}^{A-2} \hat{V}_i^{\mathrm{par}}}
       {\prod_{i=0}^{A-2} \hat{V}_i^{\mathrm{dau}}}
  = 
  \prod_{i=0}^{A-2}
  \frac{\hat{V}_i^{\mathrm{par}}}{\hat{V}_i^{\mathrm{dau}}}.

For generators i > p, the crossings from nucleon i to nucleons j > i are identical in parent and daughter because neither nucleon i nor any j > i changed type. Therefore \hat{V}_i^{\mathrm{par}} = \hat{V}_i^{\mathrm{dau}} and the ratio is 1. Only generators i \leq p contribute.

The transition matrix element is the Skein amplitude at the beta-decay vertex, which is proportional to the trace ratio:

  |\mathcal{M}_q|^2
  = 
  |\mathrm{skein\_amp}|^2
  \cdot
  \left|
    \frac{\mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{N}(Z, N))}
         {\mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{N}(p+1, n-1))}
  \right|^2

where \mathrm{skein\_amp} = q^{1/2} - q^{-1/2}. \square
prop:hadron-half-life:
Proposition Hadron half-life from the q-deformed transition amplitude. A nucleus displaced from the valley of stability (integer stability) undergoes beta decay. The substrate parameter q (substrate parameter) governs the half-life via the q-deformed transition amplitude.

Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be the Descartes universe with substrate parameter q, and let \mathcal{N}(Z, N) (stable nucleus) be a nucleus with proton displacement \delta p = p - p_{\mathrm{stab}}(A) from the valley of stability. The beta-decay half-life is

  t_{1/2}(p, A)
  = 
  \frac{\ln 2}{\Gamma_\beta(p, A)},
  \qquad
  \Gamma_\beta(p, A)
  = 
  \frac{|\mathcal{W}_2(q)|^2 \cdot \mu_0}{2\pi^3}
   \cdot 
  [2]_q
   \cdot 
  |\mathcal{M}_q|^2
   \cdot 
  f(Q),

where \mathcal{W}_2(q) = t_1 + c_{\mathrm{em}}\,t_2 is the weak vertex form factor of the mediating torus knot T_{3,5} (beta decay as crossing change) under the two-term Lagrangian trace: t_1 = \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Markov}}((\sigma_1\sigma_2)^5) in H_3(q), and t_2 is the trace of the same braid against the connected all-pairs charge insertion with coefficient c_{\mathrm{em}}; [2]_q = q + q^{-1} is the \mathrm{SU}_q(2) fundamental dimension; |\mathcal{M}_q|^2 is the parent/daughter Markov-trace ratio; and f(Q) \propto Q^5 is the Sargent phase-space integral in the Q-value (transition energy). The decay rate depends on q, the dimensional scale \mu_0, and, through c_{\mathrm{em}}\,t_2, on the coefficient c_{\mathrm{em}} and the charges on the three vertex strands. When the three vertex strands carry one charge type, t_2 = 0 and the rate depends only on q and \mu_0.

prop:hadron-q-self-correction:
Proposition Effective substrate parameter: hadron self-deformation of q. The substrate parameter q \colon M \to k^\times (substrate parameter) is a field, not a background constant. A hadron (hadron) is a multi-component knot composite containing internal Hopf junctions and crossings. It perturbs the local value of q through its topological linking structure. The effective substrate parameter observed by a nucleus is

  q_{\mathrm{eff}}(p, n)
  = 
  q_0 +  \delta q(p, n),

with background value q_0 and hadron self-deformation \delta q(p, n).

Let \mathcal{N}(Z, N) = Z\mathfrak{p} \oplus N\mathfrak{n} be a nucleus (stable nucleus). The signed crossing excess—the imbalance between positive (\mathfrak{p}--\mathfrak{p}) and negative (\mathfrak{n}--\mathfrak{n}) Hopf crossings—determines the self-deformation of the substrate parameter:

  \delta q(p, n)
  = 
  \frac{\ell_{\mathrm{net}}(p, n)}{A^2}
  \cdot \hbar_q^2,
  \qquad
  \ell_{\mathrm{net}}(p, n)
  = 
  \binom{p}{2} - \binom{n}{2}
  = 
  \frac{p(p-1) - n(n-1)}{2},

where \hbar_q = 1 - q_0^{-1} is the quantum Planck constant. For neutron-rich nuclei (n > p), \ell_{\mathrm{net}} < 0 and the local q drops; for proton-rich nuclei, \ell_{\mathrm{net}} > 0 and q rises.

prop:skein-coulomb-enhancement:
Proposition Coulomb enhancement from electron-proton Skein crossings. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a Descartes universe with substrate parameter q. Consider the beta decay \mathcal{N}(Z, N) \to \mathcal{N}(p\!+\!1, n\!-\!1) + e^- + \nu^{\sigma}. The emitted electron e^- crosses each of the Z = p + 1 proton strands of the daughter nucleus as it exits the Hopf link. The q-deformed wedge product \wedge_q (crossing asymmetry) assigns weight q to each positive electron-proton crossing. This produces a coherent product that multiplies the decay rate by the Skein-Coulomb enhancement factor:

  F_q(Z, E)
  = 
  \frac{2\pi\eta_q}{1 - e^{-2\pi\eta_q}}

The q-deformed Sommerfeld parameter is:

  \eta_q
  = 
  \alpha_{\mathrm{EM}}(q)
  \cdot \frac{Z}{\beta_e}

The EM coupling projection is \alpha_{\mathrm{EM}}(q) = q^{-1}/([9]_q \cdot [10]_q) (EM coupling projection). The velocity of the emitted electron is \beta_e = v_e / c.

Derivation. Evaluate the canonical action \mathfrak{S}_q (canonical action) on the full outgoing state \psi = e^- \cup \mathcal{N}(p\!+\!1, n\!-\!1). This decomposes as:

  \mathfrak{S}_q\big|_\psi
  = 
  \mathfrak{S}_q\big|_{\mathcal{N}}
  + 
  \sum_{j=1}^{Z} \mathcal{S}_{e\text{-}p_j}
  + 
  \mathfrak{S}_q\big|_{e^-}

The middle sum runs over all electron-proton crossings. Each crossing contributes a Skein weight \mathcal{S}_{e\text{-}p_j}(q) = q. This is a positive crossing between two like-charge constituents. The electron radial wave function picks up a phase e^{i\delta_\ell} at each proton. The phase shift is:

  \delta_\ell
  = 
  \arg \Gamma(\ell + 1 + i\eta_q).

Form the coherent product of Z such scattering amplitudes. Sum over partial waves \ell and integrate over the electron energy spectrum. This yields:

  |\psi_e(0)|^2_{\text{Coulomb}}
  = 
  |\psi_e(0)|^2_{\text{free}}
   \times 
  F_q(Z, E).

The decay rate is directly proportional to |\psi_e(0)|^2, the electron wave function at the nuclear origin. Thus, F_q multiplies the leading-order rate.

Remark Magnitude, transition classes, and what the QOU predicts. The leading-order half-life formula (hadron half-life) evaluates the Skein polynomial on the nucleus alone. It treats the emitted electron as a free particle. However, the electron e^- (electron) traverses the Coulomb field of Z protons as it exits the nucleus. Each electron-proton crossing carries a Skein weight. Evaluate the Skein polynomial on the full outgoing link e^- \cup \mathcal{N}(Z, N). This generates the Coulomb enhancement.

Evaluate precisely the same Skein polynomial on the complete outgoing link rather than truncating at the weak vertex.

Magnitude. Average the integrated Coulomb enhancement over the electron energy spectrum. This yields a large, Z-dependent factor.

See Table: Skein-Coulomb enhancement factors.

These enhancements change decay rates by factors of 1.4 to 5. Shell closures, pairing, and deformation modify the Gamow--Teller strength \sigma_{\mathrm{GT}} at the individual-nucleus level.

Transition classes. The nuclear matrix element |\mathcal{M}_q|^2 varies by six orders of magnitude across the verification set. Measured \log ft values (NNDC/ENSDF) classify the transitions.

See Table: Beta-decay classification.

The QOU framework dictates the q-dependent modulation of each transition class via [2]_q, \tanh(\ln q), and \sigma_{\mathrm{GT}}. It does not predict the absolute matrix element from the leading-order Hecke computation alone. Predicting |\mathcal{M}_q|^2 for individual nuclei requires resolving the discrete shell structure. The precise quantum numbers of the parent and daughter nuclear states must be specified.

Predictions of the QOU. Within a single transition class of fixed \log ft, the QOU correctly predicts:

  1. The q-dependent scale: The factor (q + q^{-1})(q - q^{-1})^5 sets the overall decay-rate scale entirely from q.
  2. The A-dependence: This gives t_{1/2} \propto A^{5/3} at fixed |\delta p| and fixed transition class.
  3. The q-sensitivity: The prediction is \partial \ln \Gamma / \partial \ln q \approx 48, without free parameters.
  4. The Coulomb enhancement structure: The term F_q(Z, E) emerges directly from the Skein crossing weights. This unifies the electromagnetic and weak interactions through the single deformation parameter q.
  5. The self-deformation: A differential \Delta q_{\mathrm{eff}} correction induced by the hadron linking structure is observed.
rem:groebner-nf-computation:
Remark Gröbner--Shirshov normal form computation with quotient ideals. The Gröbner--Shirshov normal form \mathcal{N}(Z, N) of a nucleus in H_A(q) is a formal sum over reduced braid words:

  \mathcal{N}(Z, N)
  = 
  \sum_{w \in \mathrm{supp}} c_w \cdot w.

Each amplitude c_w \in \mathbb{Z}[q^{1/2}, q^{-1/2}] is an exact Laurent polynomial in the substrate parameter q. The support \mathrm{supp} \subset S_A consists of reduced words in the symmetric group.
